acidBaseSetPoint.title: What the air does to blood
acidBaseSetPoint.subtitle: Carbon dioxide sets the acidity; bicarbonate is the only lever against it

hint.earth: Twenty-four units of bicarbonate against forty of carbon dioxide. This is the ratio every mammal on Earth defends, and it lands on 7.39.
hint.defendEarthPh: Same pH, Pandoran air. The bicarbonate needed is three times a mammal's, and a reserve that large carries an osmotic bill the tissue cannot pay.
hint.nativeSetPoint: Drop the target instead of raising the reserve, and the numbers become affordable. Nothing in canon states this value; it is what the arithmetic leaves standing.
hint.earthAirShock: Clean air washes the carbon dioxide out in under a minute. The bicarbonate takes days to follow, and in the gap the blood turns alkaline.

verdict.lethalAcidosis: Past the acid limit. Enzymes misfold and the heart loses its rhythm.
verdict.compensatedLow: Acid by our standards, and stable — if the proteins were built for it.
verdict.alkalosis: Alkaline. Vessels in the brain constrict and calcium falls out of solution.
verdict.lethalAlkalosis: Past the alkaline limit. Tetany, then apnoea.

loadNote.ordinary: A mammalian reserve. Nothing strains to carry it.
loadNote.elevated: Well above ours, and within reach — some cave bats live near the bottom of this band.
loadNote.unaffordable: This much bicarbonate drags water into the plasma, strips chloride, and starts precipitating calcium phosphate in soft tissue.

acidBaseSetPoint.earthCostNote: Bicarbonate required for a terrestrial pH at this carbon dioxide tension.

aria.lethalAcidosis: Blood acidity past the survivable limit at this carbon dioxide tension and bicarbonate reserve.
aria.compensatedLow: Blood held stable below the terrestrial set-point by a raised bicarbonate reserve.
aria.terrestrialNormal: Blood at the terrestrial acidity set-point.
aria.alkalosis: Blood turned alkaline as carbon dioxide falls faster than bicarbonate can clear.
aria.lethalAlkalosis: Blood alkalinity past the survivable limit.

acidBaseSetPoint.modelNote: Henderson-Hasselbalch with measured plasma constants. Canon states no Pandoran blood pH, so the native set-point here is reconstruction, not reporting.

oxygenAffinity.title: Handing the oxygen over
oxygenAffinity.subtitle: A pigment is judged on what it releases, not what it holds

hint.thin: The muscle has taken nearly everything. Superb for a chase, and no margin at all if delivery stumbles.
hint.workable: Most of the load handed over, some still in reserve. This is what a working body looks like.
hint.ample: Barely tapped. The blood is returning almost as full as it left, which is what resting looks like.

extraction.sparing: A light draw. Most of the cargo goes back unused.
extraction.moderate: A working extraction, of the kind sustained effort needs.
extraction.aggressive: Nearly everything, stripped in one pass.

loadingNote.plateau: Loading sits on the flat top of the curve, where affinity barely matters.
loadingNote.limited: Now the pigment cannot fill even at the lung. Loading has become the limit.

aria.thin: The pigment gives up nearly all its oxygen in one pass, leaving no reserve in the returning blood.
aria.workable: The pigment gives up most of its oxygen and keeps a usable margin.
aria.ample: The pigment gives up only a small share of its oxygen.

oxygenAffinity.modelNote: Hill binding with a Bohr shift. Alveolar tensions are derived from canonical atmospheric figures; the pigment itself is never named in canon beyond being iron-based.

radiatorHeat.title: The ceiling on effort
radiatorHeat.subtitle: Sustained power is capped by what the radiators can shed

hint.rainforestChase: Saturated air, so the evaporation bar barely exists. Everything rides on convection, which is the one term the dense atmosphere inflates.
hint.eclipseTotality: The sky goes cold and the air falls. Now the radiators are a liability, and the animal's problem is shutting them.
hint.montaneWind: Cold air moving fast strips heat faster than any body this size can make it. Shelter and bulk, or nothing.

balance.overheating: Above the ceiling. The core is climbing and the chase has a deadline.
balance.steady: Inside the ceiling. This can be held indefinitely.
balance.mustConserve: Far under the ceiling. The radiators have to be shut or the body simply drains.

radiatorHeat.clockNote: Until the core has risen two degrees.

deficitNote.closed: Nearly closed. Sweat will not evaporate, so it cools nothing.
deficitNote.open: Open enough for evaporation to matter.

airGainNote.denser: Advantage over Earth-density air at the same speed.
airGainNote.thinner: Penalty against Earth-density air at the same speed.

aria.overheating: Heat production exceeds everything the body can shed, so the core temperature is rising.
aria.steady: Heat production sits within what the body can shed, so the effort can be sustained.
aria.mustConserve: Heat loss far exceeds production, so the body must close its radiators to hold temperature.

radiatorHeat.modelNote: Newton cooling with a density-scaled coefficient, Stefan-Boltzmann radiation, and vapour-deficit evaporation. Canon gives no metabolic rate, core temperature, or radiator area for any native species.

sulfideElectron.title: Poison, or fuel
sulfideElectron.subtitle: The same molecule, and the only difference is how fast a body can process it

hint.human: Every enzyme needed is already here — a body makes its own sulfide as a signal. There is simply no capacity, and past a few hundred parts per million the surplus reaches the respiratory chain.
hint.exopack: The biology is unchanged. The mask takes the sulfide out before the lung ever sees it, which is why it works at all.
hint.sulfideSpringFish: Real convergence, measured in Mexican sulfur springs: a modified binding site and an expanded cascade. Sized for a spring, not for a whole atmosphere.
hint.pandoranNative: Put the cliff above what the air delivers and the poison becomes a supplement — a few per cent of the respiratory electrons, arriving free with every breath.

fateNote.trace: Cleared without effort, and too little to be worth anything.
fateNote.supplement: Cleared, and the electrons go to work. This is food.
fateNote.nearCapacity: The cascade is nearly saturated. A little more and free sulfide runs away.
fateNote.arrest: Past the cascade and onto the oxygen-reduction site. Every mitochondrion stops at once.

sulfideElectron.chainNote: Share of cytochrome c oxidase still reducing oxygen.

cascadeNote.under: Within capacity, so free sulfide stays near zero.
cascadeNote.over: Over capacity. Sulfide now accumulates with nothing to stop it.

energyNote.gain: Real energy, arriving with the air.

aria.trace: Sulfide cleared easily by the disposal cascade, too little to supply useful energy.
aria.supplement: Sulfide cleared by the cascade and feeding electrons into the respiratory chain.
aria.nearCapacity: The disposal cascade is close to saturation and free sulfide is beginning to accumulate.
aria.arrest: Free sulfide has reached cytochrome c oxidase and the respiratory chain has stopped.

sulfideElectron.modelNote: A saturable clearance cascade against competitive inhibition of the oxygen-reduction site. Enzymes and exposure rungs are real; native capacity is inference — canon says only that the sulfide is there and that it kills us.
